            1. 1. Claude codes every booking.It reads the customer's own words and picks the problem, asking one question when unsure.
            2. 2. Staple plans the trucks.Which technician takes each call, in what order, and what each truck loads tonight.
            3. 3. People act before 08:00.The parts room loads, the call center and dispatch ring customers, the buyer chases back-orders.

            The evidence

            9 cards over all 92 held-back days, on the call-taker's booked codes, so they measure the planning apart from the reading. Each has its chart, the table the chart is drawn from, and its control.

            Who takes the call

            Every held-back day replayed with the same made-up sick calls, breakdowns and priority changes. Staple sends each call to the technician with the lowest expected cost: drive and repair minutes, plus a repeat visit times the chance that technician's skill or truck fails it, placing first the call with most to lose?. Shuffling the technicians' skills drops it to 84.4%, below the parts-only rule's 84.6%, so what skills add to that rule comes from knowing who is good at what. Shuffling the history behind the parts odds it reads leaves it at 86.8%, so that control does not fall back. The parts judgment earns most of its gain during the day, by sending a call that comes in or is moved to a truck already loaded for that appliance. That needs only what each appliance usually needs, which the shuffle keeps. Calls moved by a sick day or a breakdown were fixed first time 77.9% of the time, against 69.6% for the current rules. A rolled call? counts as not fixed.

            What a fleet does with this: keep the routing system dispatch already owns, and hand it this expected-cost score for each technician and call, so its routes carry the skill and parts judgment.

            What to load tonight

            Each night the balanced truck ranks every part by its worth? per unit of space. It covers 90.2% of jobs for $111.94 a truck-day?, against 78.6% and $180.16 for today's fixed stock, while holding $3,076 against $3,162. Three tests of that gain follow. Loaded from shuffled history, the control?, it still covers 87.0% for $136.46 and keeps 64% of the saving. So that share comes from loading each truck for the appliances it will meet tomorrow, and the rest from the predictor's odds for each model family and problem. The balanced truck also fills 89 units of space where today's stock uses 81; held to today's space it covers 88.7% for $126.87. And the saving leans on the made-up $2 for moving one part: at $5 it costs $144.82, at $10 it costs $153.82, at $20 it costs $154.99, each still under today's $180.16.

            What a fleet does with this: switch the overnight load from a fixed stock list to tomorrow's booked calls, so the parts room works from a load sheet per truck, like the one the plan opens beside the board.

            Claude coding the bookings

            Claude Haiku 5.5 (claude-haiku-5-5) reads the customer's own words and picks a problem code with a confidence. On that code alone its 3-part list covers 68.2% of jobs, against 71.6% for the booked code? and 51.4% for a plain keyword matcher. These bookings describe their problems in only 456 ways, so each figure is a score over that many readings and not over thousands of separate ones. When Claude is unsure it asks one question. With a customer who always picks the matching answer, its list covers 70.3%, an upper bound. With random replies, the control, it covers 66.5%. A real customer lands between the two. Shuffling Claude's answers between bookings drops its list to 32.5%. The second chart holds Claude to the confidence it states. Where it states 0.90 to 1.00, its first reading matches the booked code on 98.5% of bookings. Where it states 0.00 to 0.50, on 17.1%. Where it states 0.50 to 0.70 it matches on 100.0% of 485 bookings, as often as the surer bands, and Staple still asks its question there. Staple asks below 0.7, so that line is cautious on this data. It is a stated choice and it is not moved to fit, because it would then be tuned on the jobs it is scored on. The answers are saved with the code, so these pages rebuild without a key.

            What a fleet does with this: let Claude code the bookings and ask its one question at the moment of booking, and keep a person on the few calls its question cannot settle.

            Back-orders to chase first

            A back-order? starts on one day and ships on another, so the list is made again every day: the days left count down, and a part drops off the day it ships. For each stuck part the list forecasts the calls that will need it before it ships, from training history only, and how many have no truck nearby holding one. Across the 110 back-orders that shipped inside the held-back days it expected 950.4 calls and 81.3 stuck; the days then brought 961 and 85. A single booking is flagged when its odds of needing a stuck part reach 10%. Of 13,587 held-back bookings, 62 were flagged and 8 of those were stuck. So the count can be forecast and the single booking cannot: a flag is a reason to warn a customer, never a prediction for that call.

            What a fleet does with this: expedite from the top of this list, and move spares toward the zones where no truck holds one.

            Claude as the buyer

            Each back-ordered part on each held-back day is one case, 936 in all. The buyer sends the calls anyway, expedites the part, moves one from another truck or rebooks the waiting calls, and the engine prices all four in expected dollars from training history. A decider? is charged the action it names, and loses what that costs over the cheapest action. Sending anyway every time loses $30,659, expediting every time $70,926, and the control? $28,748: it takes the cheapest action for another case's facts, so a small loss has to come from reading each case's own. A Claude model decides the same cases from lookups that return counts, days and odds and never a price, so it has to work the dollars out itself, and its words are held to the instructions too. Claude Haiku 5.5 (claude-haiku-5-5) picked an action as cheap as any on 929 of 936 and lost $753, $0.80 a decision. It got 7 wrong. On 7 of them its choice is the cheapest once expediting is charged the calls that come after the early ship day, where the instructions say before, so one misreading explains them all. Every action it named could be carried out. Asking cost $0.39, which is 0.04 cents a decision. The part, the ship day or a truck of a move is missing from 7 of its notes, and stray markup follows the reason in 16 of its replies. Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) picked an action as cheap as any on 936 of 936 and lost nothing. Every action it named could be carried out. Asking cost $12.71, which is 1.36 cents a decision. The part, the ship day or a truck of a move is missing from none of its notes, and stray markup follows the reason in none of its replies. Claude Opus 5.5 lost $753 less than Claude Haiku 5.5 and cost $12.32 more to ask. Each day's buyer list shows Claude Opus 5.5's decisions, because it lost the fewest dollars. Here the cheapest action is plain arithmetic, so no decider can beat the engine and a model can only tie it. The card tests something narrower: whether a model handed only the facts reaches that action, at what price, and with a note a person could send. Nothing here sends a note. The decisions are saved with the code, so these pages rebuild without a key.

            What a fleet does with this: let a model work each back-order from the same lookups and draft the note, score its choices against the arithmetic every night, and keep the buyer's sign-off on every note before it goes out.

            Which parts to carry

            The predictor ranks parts by how often they fixed the same model family and problem, and leans? on the wider appliance group when a family's history is thin. Three parts on the carry list? cover 71.6% of held-back jobs; the national top three cover 40.3%. Shuffling the history drops the predictor to 38.5%. Scored again with the held-back jobs already in its history, it covers 71.9%, +0.3 points. That gap is what holding the days back is worth. It is small here because the invented failure rates never change; on real history it is the gap to watch.

            What a fleet does with this: rank each booked call's parts by model family and problem rather than by national usage, and feed those lists to the overnight load.

            Where repeat visits come from

            On today's trucks, a missing part causes 67% of repeat visits?. Washers are worst: 29 of every 100 washer jobs need a repeat visit because a part was not on board.

            What a fleet does with this: start the pilot on washers, where a missing part costs the most repeat visits.

            How long a repair waits for its parts

            A repair whose truck lacked a part waits for it: the part is ordered, the supplier takes its lead time, and the technician comes back. Those days are the parts cycle time?. In the held-back history 21.4% of repairs waited, 3.38 days each. Replayed over the same days, the current rules? leave 20.4% waiting and Staple 4.0%. Spread over every repair, the wait falls from 0.69 days to 0.15. Staple changes how many repairs wait, not the supplier's days: every row draws on the same made-up lead times, and no way of handing out calls shortens them. A repair that still waits under Staple waits 3.76 days against 3.40. That is longer because 12.9% of its waits are on a part no center can ship, against 7.0%. A truck cannot load a part on back-order?, so those are the waits a better load does not remove. Of the other rows, 2 wait less than Staple without knowing who is good at what: parts only, balanced loads fixes 84.6% of calls on the first visit and Staple with shuffled skills (control) 84.4%, against Staple's 87.0%.

            What a fleet does with this: measure it from two days the history already holds, the order day and the repeat-visit day, and send the back-ordered waits to the buyer's list, because loading cannot remove them.

            Each gain against its control

            A control? is a method run again with one link in its data broken. Where the gain goes with the link, it came from the link. 4 of these 8 controls fall back, each keeping under 25% of its gain. 4 controls do not: top-up from shuffled history keeps 35%; balanced from shuffled history keeps 64%; Staple with shuffled-history parts odds (control) keeps 92%; Staple on shuffled history (control) keeps 93%. Each of them shuffles the history, and that shuffle keeps what every appliance usually needs. So the share a control keeps is what knowing tomorrow's appliances is worth, and the rest is what the links to model family and problem add. The carry list's own control falls back because the list it is measured against, the national top parts, already knows the appliance.

            What a fleet does with this: run every control on its own history before crediting a gain, and credit a gain to a link only where breaking that link takes the gain away.

            How a fleet would adopt it

            1. Back-test on its own history. The same replay on real calls, parts and technicians, before any truck changes. If the gains vanish there, it stops here.
            2. Pilot one region. Load and dispatch one region by this plan for six weeks against a matched region left as it is, and compare first-time fix, parts-caused repeat visits and stock value.
            3. Roll out region by region. Each region goes live only after the one before it beat its match.

            What this shows, and what it does not

            The plan for each day runs on Claude's codes, over one invented week. The scorecard and the evidence run on the call-taker's booked codes for all 92 held-back days, so they measure the planning apart from the reading. Every result reproduces from one seed, and each gain is shown beside a control that breaks the link it should come from: 4 of the 8 fall back, and the last evidence card names the ones that do not. None of it shows the gains on a real fleet, because the history is invented. The method cuts 9 corners on purpose, each marked in the code and listed on the methods page with the upgrade that would lift it. Among them: counting instead of a trained model, zone-to-zone drive times instead of road routing, and a call-by-call night plan instead of a solver.

            Run it yourself

            Staple needs Python 3.10 or newer and installs nothing. python run.py invents the history and builds every figure and page here. python check.py then checks them, and plants faults to prove its checks can fail. The code is at github.com/AceP2317/staple, and the instruction manual walks through a first run.

            Written in Python, SQL and JavaScript: 17 Python files invent the history, predict parts, load trucks, ask Claude, replay dispatch, write these pages and check it all; 16 SQL files hold the tables and the 15 metric queries; 2 JavaScript files run the hints and switches. Beside them, 7 Bash scripts run the checks before each commit, and 3 HTML files and 1 CSS file lay out the pages. Nothing is installed beyond Python. Every figure in the evidence comes from the queries in sql/metrics/, and the plan is the record the dispatch replay kept.
